questions.q: Priya's compass sits under a stretched wire. When she closes the switch, the needle swings away from north. She opens the switch, slides a wooden ruler between the wire and the compass, and closes the switch again. What will she see?
questions.a: The needle swings again, as the effect acts through the wood
o: The needle swings again, as the effect acts through the wood
The needle stays still, as the wood blocks the magnetic effect
The needle swings only after she opens the switch again
The needle swings the other way, as the wood reverses the effect

questions.q:
Kabir builds a circuit from a cell, a switch and a long wire, with no lamp in it.
(a) How can he use a magnetic compass to find out whether current flows when the switch is ON?
(b) He leaves the switch ON for a long time. The needle's deflection slowly becomes smaller, though nothing has been moved, every joint is firm and the wire stays cool to the touch. Give a reason based on the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Place the compass under (or near) the wire and switch ON. If the needle deflects from its original direction, current is flowing, because a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it. (b) A cell connected for a long time weakens and supplies less current. Less current gives a weaker magnetic field, so the needle deflects less.
s: Part (a): compass near the wire; deflection on switching ON shows current
Part (b): the cell weakens, gives less current, so a weaker field and smaller deflection

questions.q:
After testing a wire, a compass and a switch several times, a group writes three statements.
Statement 1: The magnetic field around the wire disappears as soon as the current stops flowing.
Statement 2: After the switch is moved to OFF, the needle stays at its deflected position because the wire remains magnetised.
Statement 3: The region around the wire in which the compass needle is deflected is said to have a magnetic field.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A compass needle placed under a current-carrying wire returns to its original direction as soon as the switch is moved to OFF.
Reason (R): The compass needle is itself a tiny magnet.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A 2 m wire runs along a lab bench from a cell to a switch. Compass P is placed under the wire close to the cell and compass Q under the wire close to the switch. Which needles deflect when the switch is closed?
questions.a: Both P and Q, since the whole wire carries the current
o: Both P and Q, since the whole wire carries the current
Only P, since the current is strongest next to the cell
Only Q, since the switch is where the current starts
Neither, since a straight wire needs to be coiled first

questions.q: True or False? 'A copper wire can deflect a compass needle even though copper is not attracted by a magnet.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The needle is not deflected because copper is magnetic; it is deflected by the magnetic field that the electric current produces around the wire. Any conductor carrying current produces such a field, and it disappears when the current stops.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the deflection comes from the field produced by the current, not from the copper being magnetic

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the conclusion it supports in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Needle deflects when the switch is ON and returns when it is OFF | a. No current is flowing in the circuit
2. Needle deflects even with a sheet of cardboard between wire and compass | b. The field exists only while current flows
3. Needle does not move when the switch is ON, and the circuit's lamp stays dark | c. The compass was outside the region where the wire's effect is felt
4. Needle deflects under the wire but not when the compass is carried to the far side of the room | d. The magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials
Arjun claims: 'If the compass needle under the wire does not move when I switch ON, the cell must be dead.' Is his claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. A needle that does not move shows that no current is flowing, and a dead cell (whose chemicals are used up) is one possible cause. But it is not the only cause: a loose connection, a broken wire or a faulty switch would also leave the circuit open, so no current flows and no magnetic field is produced. He must check the connections before blaming the cell.
s: Verdict: partly right
No deflection means no current, so no magnetic field
Other causes of no current: loose connection, broken wire or faulty switch (open circuit)

questions.q: Sana's compass, lying under a wire on her desk, has swung away from north. She suspects that the swing may be caused by a bar magnet left in the drawer under the desk, and not by the current in the wire. Which single test settles the question?
questions.a: Move the switch to OFF and see whether the needle returns
o: Move the switch to OFF and see whether the needle returns
Slide a cardboard sheet between the wire and the compass
Move the compass a few cm along under the same wire
Keep the switch ON for five more minutes and watch the needle

questions.q: Differentiate between the magnetic field of a bar magnet and that of a straight current-carrying wire. Give one way in which they are alike and one way in which they differ.
questions.a: Alike: both have a region around them where a magnetic effect can be felt, for example by the deflection of a compass needle. Differ: the bar magnet's field is always present, while the wire's field exists only while current flows through it and disappears when the current stops.
s: Alike: both have a region where a compass is deflected (a magnetic field)
Differ: the wire's field exists only while current flows; the magnet's is always present

questions.q: A student lists four observations from her electricity practicals under the heading 'Evidence of the magnetic effect of electric current'. Which observation does NOT belong under that heading?
questions.a: A nichrome wire feels warm after current flows for 30 s
o: A nichrome wire feels warm after current flows for 30 s
A compass under a wire swings each time the switch is ON
Iron clips cling to a coiled nail only while it is connected
A compass beside a coil swings the other way when the cell is turned round

questions.a: (i) Current in the wire produces a magnetic field around it, and the compass needle, itself a tiny magnet, is deflected by it. (ii) When the current stops, the magnetic field disappears, so nothing deflects the needle and it returns to its original direction. (iii) Glass is non-magnetic, and a magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials kept in between.
s: (i) current produces a magnetic field that deflects the tiny-magnet needle
(ii) the field disappears when current stops
(iii) the effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as glass

questions.q: Compare an electric lamp and a magnetic compass as ways of finding out whether current flows in a circuit. Analyse them on five points: (1) how each must be placed, (2) what it shows when current flows, (3) what it shows when current stops, (4) the effect of electric current each one relies on, (5) one situation where the compass is the more practical choice.
questions.a: (1) The lamp has to be connected into the circuit; the compass is only placed near (for example, under) a wire. (2) When current flows, the lamp's filament is heated and it glows; the compass needle deflects from its original direction. (3) When current stops, the lamp goes dark; the needle returns to its original direction because the field disappears. (4) The lamp relies on the heating effect of current; the compass relies on the magnetic effect. (5) When the wire cannot be opened up to add a lamp, for example a wire behind a wooden or plastic cover, a compass held near it still works, because the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials.
s: (1) lamp connected into the circuit, compass only placed near a wire
(2) lamp glows, needle deflects
(3) lamp goes dark, needle returns as the field disappears
(4) lamp = heating effect, compass = magnetic effect
(5) compass works through a non-magnetic cover without opening the circuit

questions.q:
Rohini's group in Nagpur tested a wire stretched over a compass, using the same cell and the same compass throughout, and kept this record.
Trial | Switch | Placed between wire and compass | Needle
1 | ON | nothing | deflected
2 | OFF | nothing | in original direction
3 | ON | thin cardboard sheet | deflected
4 | ON | plastic lid | deflected
5 | ON | nothing | in original direction
6 | OFF | plastic lid | in original direction
(a) What do Trials 1 and 2 together show?
(b) What do Trials 3 and 4 show about the materials used?
(c) Trial 5 has the same settings as Trial 1 but a different result. Give the most likely explanation and say what the group should check.
(d) Rohini wants to write: 'The wire acts like a magnet only while current flows; its effect passes through cardboard and plastic; and a thicker cover gives a weaker effect.' Decide which parts of her sentence the record supports, naming the trials you rely on.
questions.a: (a) The wire has a magnetic effect only while current flows: the needle deflects when the switch is ON and returns when it is OFF. (b) The magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as cardboard and plastic. (c) No current was flowing in Trial 5, so there was no magnetic field to deflect the needle. The circuit was probably open (a loose connection, a wire slipped off the cell holder, or a faulty switch); the group should check every connection, and only then the cell. (d) The first two parts are supported: Trials 1 and 2 show the effect exists only while current flows, and Trials 3 and 4 show cardboard and plastic do not stop it. The third part is not supported: the thickness of the cover was never changed, and the record only says 'deflected', not by how much. Trial 5 must be set aside as a broken circuit, not used as evidence against her.
s: Part (a): magnetic effect only while current flows
Part (b): the effect acts through non-magnetic cardboard and plastic
Part (c): no current flowed (open circuit, e.g. loose connection); check the connections
Part (d): first two parts supported by Trials 1-4; the thickness claim is not tested; Trial 5 set aside

questions.q:
A student in Pune has built a battery-powered model house for a science fair. Three of its wires run hidden inside a plastic channel on a cardboard wall, and she must find which one feeds the model's porch lamp without opening the channel. She holds a compass flat against the channel over each wire in turn, first with every switch in the model OFF, then with only the porch-lamp switch ON.
Wire | Needle with all switches OFF | Needle with only the porch lamp ON
X | original direction | original direction
Y | original direction | deflected
Z | original direction | original direction
(a) Decide which wire feeds the porch lamp.
(b) Why does the compass work even though the wires are inside a plastic channel?
(c) Why did she first take readings with every switch OFF?
questions.a: (a) Wire Y, because only Y deflects the needle, and only when the porch lamp is ON, that is, only when current flows to the lamp. (b) Plastic is non-magnetic, and the magnetic effect of the current acts through non-magnetic materials, so the field reaches the compass. (c) With every switch OFF, no wire carries current, so no wire should deflect the needle. This checks that nothing else (such as a nearby magnet) is moving it, so the deflection with the lamp ON can only come from the current in Y.
s: Part (a): Wire Y, the only one that deflects, and only with the lamp ON
Part (b): the effect acts through the non-magnetic plastic
Part (c): an all-OFF reading shows no deflection without current, so the later deflection is due to the lamp's current

questions.q:
In a circuit of a cell, a switch, a lamp and connecting wires, a compass under one wire deflects while the lamp glows.
(a) The lamp is taken out and its two wires are joined directly. Will the compass still deflect when the switch is ON? Why?
(b) Instead, the cell is taken out and the gap is left open. Will the compass deflect now? Why?
questions.a: (a) Yes. The circuit is still complete, so current still flows through the wire and produces a magnetic field that deflects the needle; the lamp was not needed for the magnetic effect. (b) No. Without the cell the circuit is open and has no source, so no current flows and there is no magnetic field.
s: Part (a): yes, current still flows in the complete circuit, so a field is produced
Part (b): no, no current flows, so no field

questions.q: A student's notebook ends with this conclusion: 'So the magnetic field of the wire was felt through the plastic, but only while current was flowing.' Describe a set-up, and the two observations, that would lead to exactly this conclusion.
questions.a: Set-up: a wire connected to a cell through a switch, with a compass placed beneath it and a plastic sheet (or lid) placed between the wire and the compass. Observation 1: with the switch ON, the needle deflects even though the plastic is in between, so the field is felt through the plastic. Observation 2: with the switch OFF, and the plastic still in place, the needle returns to its original direction, so the field exists only while current flows.
s: Set-up with wire, cell, switch, compass and plastic between wire and compass
Switch ON with plastic in place: needle deflects
Switch OFF with plastic in place: needle returns to original direction

questions.q: Aakarsh used to think electricity and magnetism had nothing to do with each other. Justify, in five points from this chapter, the statement 'Electricity and magnetism are linked.'
questions.a: (1) A compass needle, which is a tiny magnet, deflects when current flows through a wire placed over it, so a current-carrying wire has a magnetic effect. (2) The needle returns when the current stops, showing the magnetic field is produced by the current itself. (3) Current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it; this is called the magnetic effect of electric current. (4) A coil carrying current behaves like a magnet with two poles (an electromagnet), and it attracts iron clips only while current flows. (5) Many devices use this link, such as electromagnets, electric bells, motors, fans and loudspeakers, and lifting electromagnets on cranes.
s: Compass needle (a tiny magnet) deflects near a current-carrying wire
Needle returns when current stops: the field comes from the current
States the magnetic effect of electric current
A current-carrying coil behaves as a magnet (electromagnet) only while current flows
Names devices that use the link (bell, motor, fan, loudspeaker, lifting electromagnet)

questions.q: In Meher's circuit the lamp stays dark when she switches ON. She checks that her compass deflects under a wire in her friend's working circuit, then places it under a wire of her own circuit: the needle does not move. What can she conclude?
questions.a: No current flows anywhere in her circuit
o: No current flows anywhere in her circuit
Current flows, but the lamp itself is faulty
Current flows, but her compass is not working
Current flows only in the wire next to the cell

questions.q:
Current flows for a short time through a nichrome wire stretched over a compass.
(a) Name two different effects of the current you could detect in this set-up.
(b) Say how you would detect each one.
questions.a: (a) The magnetic effect and the heating effect of electric current. (b) Magnetic effect: the compass needle beneath the wire deflects while current flows. Heating effect: touching the wire momentarily after switching OFF, it feels warm (nichrome offers high resistance, so some electrical energy becomes heat).
s: Part (a): magnetic effect and heating effect
Part (b): compass deflects; wire feels warm when touched momentarily

questions.q:
For a science fair in Bhopal, a team built four electromagnets from the same kind of insulated wire, using one cell or a battery of two cells, and tested each with a compass and a heap of iron paper clips.
Magnet | Turns | Cells | Inside the coil | Compass needle | Clips held
P | 50 | 1 | empty paper tube | small deflection | 0
Q | 50 | 1 | iron nail | large deflection | 4
R | 50 | 2 | iron nail | larger deflection | 9
S | 100 | 1 | iron nail | larger deflection | 7
(a) P held no clips. Was P acting as a magnet at all? Use the table to explain.
(b) Explain why R held more clips than Q.
(c) What does comparing S with Q show?
(d) For the fair they have one iron nail, but they can borrow EITHER a second cell OR enough extra wire for 100 turns, not both. Using only the table, decide which to borrow, and say what the table cannot tell them about this choice.
questions.a: (a) Yes. P still deflected the compass needle, so the current-carrying coil was acting as a magnet; without an iron core it was only too weak to hold clips. (b) R had two cells, which give a larger current than one cell, so its magnetic field was stronger. (c) With the same cell and core, doubling the turns from 50 to 100 made the electromagnet stronger (7 clips instead of 4). (d) Borrow the second cell. On the same nail, R (50 turns, 2 cells) held 9 clips while S (100 turns, 1 cell) held 7, so in these trials the extra cell helped more than the extra turns. The table cannot show whether this holds at other numbers of turns or cells: each set-up was tried only once, at one setting.
s: Part (a): yes, P deflected the compass, so it was a weak magnet without a core
Part (b): two cells give more current, so a stronger field
Part (c): more turns, same cell and core, gives a stronger magnet
Part (d): borrow the cell (R 9 clips vs S 7), noting single trials at one setting cannot show it always holds

questions.q: Ravi winds 60 turns of insulated wire on a wooden pencil and another 60 turns on an iron nail, and connects each to an identical cell. Which result should he expect when he brings each near a compass?
questions.a: Both deflect the needle, the nail coil much more
o: Both deflect the needle, the nail coil much more
Only the nail coil deflects the needle at all
Both deflect the needle by the same amount
Only the pencil coil deflects, as wood lets current pass

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A coil of wire wound on an iron nail and joined to a cell through a switch can be called a temporary magnet that we can switch off.
Reason (R): A current-carrying coil behaves as a magnet only while current flows through it; it loses its magnetic effect when the current stops.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A Class 6 student says, 'A magnet is either a magnet or it is not. You cannot make a magnet that works only some of the time.'
(a) Explain how an iron nail can be made into a magnet that works only some of the time, using a cell.
(b) State the observation that shows this magnet is temporary.
questions.a: (a) Wrap insulated wire tightly around the nail as a coil and connect its ends to a cell. While current flows, the coil with its iron core behaves as a magnet (an electromagnet). (b) When the wire is disconnected and the current stops, iron paper clips that were clinging to the nail fall off: the magnetic effect is lost.
s: Part (a): coil wound on the nail and connected to a cell makes an electromagnet
Part (b): clips fall off when current stops

questions.q: End A of an electromagnet attracts the north pole of a compass needle. The cell is then turned round so that the current flows through the coil the other way. End A will now attract the ___ pole of the compass needle. (Write one word.)
questions.a: south

questions.q: Lalit tests his nail electromagnet with a compass and finds that end A is a North pole. End A holds 5 iron clips. What should he expect at end B?
questions.a: It is a South pole and it also attracts the clips
o: It is a South pole and it also attracts the clips
It is a South pole, so it pushes the iron clips away
It is also a North pole, since both its ends hold clips
It has no pole, as only one end of a coil is magnetic

questions.q:
Three statements about electromagnets are written on a revision card.
Statement 1: A current-carrying coil wound on a paper tube, with nothing inside it, can still deflect a compass needle.
Statement 2: Reversing the direction of the current through the coil reverses its North and South poles.
Statement 3: Connecting the same coil to a battery of more cells makes it a stronger magnet.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q: True or False? 'An electromagnet can be made stronger only by connecting more cells to it.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. More cells (a larger current) is one way, but increasing the number of turns of the coil also makes it stronger, and an iron core makes a coil a much stronger magnet. Correct statement: an electromagnet can be made stronger by increasing the current, the number of turns, or both.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: more turns (or an iron core) also make it stronger, not only more cells

questions.q: Differentiate between an electromagnet and a bar magnet by giving two ways in which an electromagnet can be controlled but a bar magnet cannot.
questions.a: Any two: (1) an electromagnet can be switched on and off, because its magnetic effect exists only while current flows; (2) its strength can be changed by changing the current or the number of turns; (3) its poles can be reversed by reversing the direction of the current. A bar magnet keeps the same poles and strength all the time.
s: First way of control (switch on/off, change strength, or reverse poles)
Second, different way of control

questions.q: Lakshmi has only aluminium wire, no copper wire. She wants to make an electromagnet on an iron nail for her project. Will it work?
questions.a: Yes, a current in any conducting wire makes a field
o: Yes, a current in any conducting wire makes a field
No, as only copper wire can produce a magnetic field
No, as aluminium is not a magnetic material
Yes, but only if the nail is also of aluminium

questions.q: Dia winds 50 turns of wire on a paper tube and connects it to a cell. She claims: 'This coil is already an electromagnet, even before I slide the iron nail in.' Is she right? Give evidence, and say what the nail will add.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. A current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet is an electromagnet, and her coil does behave as a magnet: it deflects compass needles placed near its ends while current flows, and the effect stops when the current stops. The iron nail is not needed to make it a magnet; it makes it a stronger one, so the compass deflection becomes much larger and the coil can then attract iron clips.
s: Verdict: yes, she is right
Evidence: the coil deflects a compass while current flows (behaves as a magnet)
The iron core only makes it stronger (more deflection, attracts clips)

questions.q:
A school puppet theatre needs magnets for five jobs. For each job, decide whether an electromagnet, a bar magnet, or neither should be used, and name the property from the chapter (or from earlier learning about magnets) that decides it.
(1) Lift an iron puppet sword off a table and drop it into a box exactly on cue.
(2) Hold the show's paper programme on a steel notice board all year, with no cells or wires.
(3) Make the same end of the magnet first attract and then push away the north pole of a small magnet hanging on a thread.
(4) Lift a light iron crown in Act 1 and a much heavier iron shield in Act 3.
(5) Pick up a crumpled sheet of aluminium foil used as a prop.
questions.a: (1) Electromagnet: it attracts iron only while current flows, so switching OFF drops the sword on cue. (2) Bar magnet: it keeps its magnetism without any current, whereas an electromagnet loses its magnetic effect as soon as the current stops. (3) Electromagnet: its poles reverse when the direction of the current is reversed, so one end can be North and then South; a bar magnet's poles are fixed. (4) Electromagnet: its strength can be raised by increasing the current (more cells) or the number of turns, so it can be made stronger for the shield. (5) Neither: aluminium is not a magnetic material, so no magnet, however strong, attracts it.
s: (1) electromagnet: releases when switched OFF
(2) bar magnet: needs no current; an electromagnet loses its magnetism without current
(3) electromagnet: poles reverse with the current
(4) electromagnet: strength raised by more current or more turns
(5) neither: aluminium is not a magnetic material

questions.q:
Kavya does five things in order with a coil of insulated wire wound on a paper tube. Explain what she observes at each step and why.
(i) She connects the coil to a cell with compasses near both ends.
(ii) She slides an iron nail into the tube.
(iii) She brings iron paper clips near the ends of the nail.
(iv) She turns the cell round, so the current flows the other way.
(v) She disconnects the cell.
questions.a: (i) Both compass needles deflect: the current-carrying coil behaves like a magnet. (ii) The deflection becomes much larger: the iron core makes the coil a stronger magnet. (iii) The clips are attracted to the ends: the strong electromagnet attracts iron. (iv) The compass needles swing to point the other way: reversing the current reverses the poles of the electromagnet (its strength stays the same). (v) The needles return to their original directions and the clips fall: the coil loses its magnetic effect when the current stops.
s: (i) needles deflect: coil acts as a magnet
(ii) much more deflection: iron core makes it stronger
(iii) clips attracted to the ends
(iv) needles point the other way: poles reversed
(v) needles return and clips fall: magnetic effect lost without current

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Kochi tested the poles of an electromagnet whose ends are marked A and B, using a compass. Their record:
Trial | Current direction | End tested | Compass pole attracted | Pole written for the end
1 | first way | A | north | South
2 | first way | B | south | South
3 | reversed | A | south | North
4 | reversed | B | (not recorded) | (not recorded)
(a) Explain why 'South' is correct for end A in Trial 1.
(b) One entry in Trials 1-3 is wrong. Find it and correct it.
(c) Work out the two missing entries of Trial 4.
(d) For a classroom display, the cell will sit in a holder that is fixed so the current always flows the first way, and the coil's wires will be taped down. The group wants to paint a permanent 'N' and 'S' on the two ends. Decide whether they should, and if so, which letter goes on which end.
questions.a: (a) The north pole of the compass is attracted to end A, and unlike poles attract each other, so end A must be a south pole. (b) Trial 2: end B attracts the south pole of the compass, so B is a North pole, not South; the two ends of an electromagnet have opposite poles. (c) With the current reversed, A is North (Trial 3), so B is South; a south pole attracts the north pole of the compass. Entries: compass pole attracted = north, pole written = South. (d) Yes, they can. The poles of an electromagnet reverse only when the direction of the current reverses (Trials 1 and 3). With the cell fixed so the current always flows the first way, the poles cannot swap: paint 'S' on end A and 'N' on end B (Trials 1 and corrected 2). A cell that weakens changes only the strength, not the poles.
s: Part (a): compass north attracted, unlike poles attract, so A is south
Part (b): Trial 2 entry should be North; the ends have opposite poles
Part (c): Trial 4: north pole attracted, end B is South
Part (d): yes, poles reverse only with the current, which is now fixed: A = S, B = N

questions.q: A student's report says: 'With the current flowing, both ends of my electromagnet attracted the north pole of the compass needle.' Show that this result cannot be correct as reported.
questions.a: Unlike poles attract, so an end that attracts the north pole of the compass needle is a south pole. If both ends attracted the north pole, both ends would be south poles. But an electromagnet, like a bar magnet, has two poles, North and South, and its two ends always have opposite polarity. So one end must attract the compass's north pole and the other its south pole; the report must contain an error in testing or recording.
s: An end attracting the compass north pole is a south pole
Both ends would then be south poles
An electromagnet has two opposite poles, so this is impossible

questions.q: Four electromagnets are wound on identical iron nails: (W) 1 cell, 50 turns; (X) 2 cells, 50 turns; (Y) 1 cell, 100 turns; (Z) 2 cells, 100 turns. Which one can you be sure is the strongest, without testing?
questions.a: Z, as it has both the larger current and more turns
o: Z, as it has both the larger current and more turns
X, as the number of cells matters more than the turns
Y, as the number of turns matters more than the cells
None, as all four are wound on the same kind of nail

questions.q:
Reema's nail electromagnet has been connected to a cell for some time. When she touches the coil, it feels warm.
(a) Which effect of electric current warms the coil?
(b) The activity instructions say to connect the wire to the cell for only a few seconds at a time. Give the reason, and say how ignoring it would affect the electromagnet.
questions.a: (a) The heating effect of electric current: the wire resists the current and some electrical energy becomes heat. (b) Keeping it connected longer makes the cell weaken quickly. A weakened cell gives less current, and less current makes the electromagnet weaker, so it would hold fewer clips.
s: Part (a): heating effect of electric current
Part (b): cell weakens quickly, less current, weaker electromagnet

questions.q: Ira's coil is connected to an old, weak battery of 3 cells; Om's identical coil is connected to 1 fresh cell. Om's coil deflects a compass more than Ira's. Ira says, 'This proves more cells do not make a stronger electromagnet.' Using the chain cells -> current -> magnetic field -> deflection, explain why her result does not disprove the rule.
questions.a: The rule is really about current: a battery of more cells gives a larger current than a single cell only when the cells are in good condition. Ira's old battery has weakened, so it supplies less current than Om's fresh cell. Less current produces a weaker magnetic field around the coil, so her compass deflects less. Her result shows the effect of the current, which is what the rule says; to test the number of cells fairly, she must use cells in the same condition.
s: Strength depends on the current; more cells give more current only if the cells are not weakened
Her weak battery gives less current, so a weaker field and less deflection
A fair test needs cells in the same condition, so the rule stands

questions.q:
On the same kind of iron nail, Aman's electromagnet (1 cell, 100 turns) and Bela's (2 cells, 50 turns) each hold 8 clips. A 1-cell, 50-turn electromagnet on that nail holds 4.
(a) Compared with the 1-cell, 50-turn magnet, what did Aman change and what did Bela change?
(b) Bela says, 'So doubling the cells and doubling the turns always have exactly the same effect.' Can these results prove that? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Aman increased the number of turns; Bela increased the current by using two cells. Each change made the electromagnet stronger. (b) No. These are single results for one nail at these particular values; they show both changes increased the strength here, but one pair of readings cannot show that the two changes always have the same effect. She would need more trials at other values.

Part (b): no, one pair of results at one setting cannot prove 'always'

questions.a: 50 and 100 turns, each with 1 cell and an iron nail

50 turns with 1 cell and 100 turns with 2 cells
50 turns with a nail and 100 turns on an empty tube
50 turns with 2 cells and 100 turns with 1 cell

questions.q:
A nail electromagnet is working with one cell. Match each change in Column I with its result in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. A second cell is added to make a battery | a. Weaker, but still a magnet
2. The connections at the cell are swapped | b. No longer a magnet at all

A crane operator at Visakhapatnam port holds a steel girder on a lifting electromagnet and must lay it gently on a truck bed. When should she switch the current OFF?
questions.a: When the girder is resting just above the truck bed
o: When the girder is resting just above the truck bed
Well before the truck, since the field takes minutes to fade
Before lifting, since the magnet holds best with no current
Only after the coil has cooled, or the girder will not drop

questions.q:
In Sumana's exhibition model, an iron nail wrapped with wire hangs from a toy crane. Mohini is puzzled because she can see a battery and wires but no magnet anywhere.
(a) Explain what turns the nail into a magnet when Sumana closes the circuit.
(b) Explain why the clips fall off as soon as she opens the circuit.
questions.a: (a) When the circuit is closed, current flows through the wire coiled around the nail. A current-carrying coil behaves as a magnet, and the iron nail inside makes it a stronger one, so the nail picks up iron clips: it is an electromagnet. (b) Opening the circuit stops the current, and the magnetic effect of the coil exists only while current flows, so the clips are no longer attracted and fall.
s: Part (a): current through the coil makes the nail an electromagnet
Part (b): no current, so the magnetic effect disappears and the clips fall

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A crane operator can drop a load of steel scrap exactly where it is needed without anyone pulling it off the magnet.
Reason (R): A lifting electromagnet stays magnetised for a few minutes after the current is switched OFF, which gives the operator time to place the load.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A scrap yard in Mandi Gobindgarh, Punjab, receives a 12,000 kg pile of mixed scrap: 9,000 kg of iron and steel, 1,800 kg of aluminium, 600 kg of copper and 600 kg of plastic. A hired crane with a lifting electromagnet carries at most 600 kg per lift, each lift takes 3 minutes, and the crane costs Rs 8,000 for any part of an hour (it is always charged for at least one full hour). A team of workers hand-sorts 1,500 kg of mixed scrap per hour and costs Rs 1,200 per hour.
Plan X: the team hand-sorts the whole pile. Plan Y: the crane first lifts out everything it can, then the team hand-sorts what is left.
(a) Which materials can the crane's electromagnet lift out of the pile, and what total mass is that? Give the reason.
(b) How many lifts does Plan Y need, and for how long is the crane used?
(c) Find the total time and the total cost of each plan.
(d) A buyer's truck arrives in 4 hours to collect the sorted iron and steel, and the yard pays the driver Rs 1,000 for every hour the truck has to wait. Decide which plan the yard should use, and name the property of the lifting electromagnet that makes Plan Y possible.
questions.a: (a) Only the iron and steel, 9,000 kg. A lifting electromagnet lifts iron and steel objects; aluminium, copper and plastic are not magnetic materials, so they stay behind. (b) 9,000 / 600 = 15 lifts; 15 x 3 = 45 minutes of crane time. (c) Plan X: 12,000 / 1,500 = 8 hours, costing 8 x 1,200 = Rs 9,600. Plan Y: 45 minutes of crane (charged as one hour, Rs 8,000) plus 3,000 / 1,500 = 2 hours of hand sorting (Rs 2,400): 2 hours 45 minutes and Rs 10,400. So Plan Y is faster but Rs 800 dearer. (d) Plan Y. Under Plan X the truck waits 8 - 4 = 4 hours, adding Rs 4,000, so Plan X costs Rs 13,600 against Plan Y's Rs 10,400, which finishes in 2 hours 45 minutes with no waiting. Plan Y works because the electromagnet attracts only the iron and steel and releases each load into a bin when the current is switched OFF.
s: Part (a): only iron and steel, 9,000 kg; the others are not magnetic
Part (b): 15 lifts, 45 minutes
Part (c): X 8 h, Rs 9,600; Y 2 h 45 min, Rs 10,400
Part (d): Plan Y once the Rs 4,000 waiting charge is added (Rs 13,600 vs Rs 10,400); magnet picks only iron/steel and releases when OFF

questions.q: A junkyard crane must pick up the steel body of an old car and drop it into a crusher. Why is a lifting electromagnet used rather than an equally strong permanent magnet?
questions.a: It can be switched off to let the car body fall
o: It can be switched off to let the car body fall
It attracts aluminium parts as well as steel ones
It does not need any electric supply to keep working
It attracts only those objects that are already hot

questions.q:
A worksheet on lifting electromagnets has three statements.
Statement 1: Lifting electromagnets are used in scrap yards but not in factories.
Statement 2: When the current is switched OFF, the magnetic field disappears and the load is released.
Statement 3: A lifting electromagnet is simply a large bar magnet hung from a crane.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: A scrap dealer claims: 'A strong permanent magnet hung from my crane would do the job better than a lifting electromagnet, because it never needs electricity.' Is the claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Wrong. It is true that a permanent magnet needs no electricity, but that is exactly the problem: its magnetism cannot be switched off, so the steel it picks up would stay stuck to it and would have to be pulled off. A lifting electromagnet attracts iron and steel only while current flows; the operator switches it ON to lift and OFF to release the load where it is needed. Its strength can also be changed by changing the current, which a permanent magnet does not allow.
s: Verdict: wrong
A permanent magnet cannot be switched off, so the load cannot be released easily
The electromagnet lifts when ON and releases when OFF (and its strength can be changed)

questions.q:
A lifting electromagnet is holding a bundle of steel rods above a loading bay when the power supply suddenly fails.
(a) What happens to the rods? Explain.
(b) Why must workers never stand under a load held by a lifting electromagnet?
questions.a: (a) The rods fall. When the current stops, the magnetic field of the electromagnet disappears, so nothing holds the steel any more. (b) The load is held only as long as current flows. If the supply fails or the switch is turned OFF by mistake, the load drops at once onto whoever is below.
s: Part (a): rods fall because the field disappears when current stops
Part (b): the load is held only while current flows, so it can drop without warning

questions.q: In one shift, a crane operator moves the switch of her lifting electromagnet 64 times in all, and every load needs one ON and one OFF. Each load is 450 kg of steel. The total mass of steel she moved in the shift is ___ kg. (Write the number in digits, without commas.)
True or False? 'A lifting electromagnet whose coil still feels warm can be too weak to lift anything.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A warm coil only shows that some current is still flowing (the heating effect). But if the cell or supply has weakened, that current is small, and the strength of an electromagnet depends on the current, so the magnet can be too weak to lift the load even though the coil is warm.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: warmth shows some current; a weakened supply gives too little current for a strong field

questions.q: The chapter says lifting electromagnets help factories and scrap yards move, lift and sort heavy metal items 'efficiently'. Give three reasons, each linked to how the electromagnet works, that support the word 'efficiently'.
questions.a: (1) No hooks, chains or tying: the switched-on electromagnet picks up iron and steel objects directly. (2) Instant release: switching the current OFF makes the field disappear, so the load drops exactly where it is wanted, with no one pulling it off. (3) Sorting in the same step: it attracts only iron and steel, so lowering it onto mixed scrap separates these metals from non-magnetic material. (Also accepted: being strong, it lifts heavy loads at once.)
s: Picks up iron/steel directly, without tying or hooking
Releases instantly when switched OFF
Attracts only iron/steel, so it sorts mixed scrap (or lifts heavy loads at once)

questions.q: A crane's lifting electromagnet can lift a 400 kg steel plate but cannot lift a 700 kg plate. Which change should help it lift the heavier plate?
questions.a: Pass a larger current through its coil
o: Pass a larger current through its coil
Reverse the direction of its current
Switch it on and off in quick turns, many times
Use fewer turns of wire in its coil

questions.q: Your class must build a working model of a lifting electromagnet crane for a school exhibition, like Sumana's. Describe your model in five parts: (1) the materials, (2) how the electromagnet is made and hung, (3) how the operator lifts and drops iron clips, (4) two changes you could make if it lifts too few clips, and (5) a quick test a visitor could do to check that there is no hidden permanent magnet in your model, with the reason it works.
questions.a: (1) An iron nail, a long piece of flexible insulated wire, an electric cell or a battery of cells, a switch, iron paper clips, and a stick or toy crane arm. (2) Wind the wire tightly around the nail as a coil, tape it, hang the nail from the crane arm in place of a hook, and connect the coil's ends to the cell through the switch. (3) Switch ON: current flows, the nail becomes an electromagnet and lifts the clips; move the arm and switch OFF over the target: the field disappears and the clips drop. (4) Use a battery of more cells to increase the current, and/or wind more turns of wire on the nail; both make the electromagnet stronger. (5) Lift some clips, then open the switch: the clips fall at once. A permanent magnet would keep holding them; only an electromagnet loses its magnetic effect the moment the current stops.
s: (1) suitable materials including iron nail, insulated wire, cell and switch
(2) coil wound on the nail, hung in place of a hook, connected through a switch
(3) ON lifts the clips, OFF releases them, with the reason
(4) more cells (current) and/or more turns
(5) switch OFF while holding clips: they fall, which a permanent magnet would not allow

questions.q: The answer is: 'Because its magnetic field disappears the moment the current stops.' Write two different questions about lifting electromagnets on cranes for which this is the correct answer, and explain briefly why it answers each one.
questions.a: Example 1: 'Why does a scrap-yard magnet drop its load when the operator flips the switch to OFF?' Switching OFF stops the current, the field disappears and nothing holds the steel. Example 2: 'Why is it dangerous to stand under a lifting electromagnet during a power cut?' The supply failing stops the current, so the field disappears and the load falls. (Other valid questions, for example why the load needs no one to pull it off, are accepted.)
s: First valid question (e.g. release on switching OFF)
Second, different valid question (e.g. power cut danger)
Explains how field disappearing answers both

questions.q:
A Class 8 team in Guwahati tested their model crane magnet, a coil wound on an iron bolt, and kept this record.
Trial | Cells | Turns | Clips lifted | Note
1 | 1 | 40 | 3 | fresh cell
2 | 2 | 40 | 7 | fresh cells
3 | 2 | 80 | 12 | fresh cells
4 | 2 | 80 | 4 | same cells, after being left ON for 30 minutes; coil feels warm
(a) Explain why Trial 2 lifted more clips than Trial 1.
(b) What does Trial 3 add to what Trial 2 showed?
(c) Trial 4 used the same set-up as Trial 3. Explain both of its observations: fewer clips, yet a warm coil.
(d) The model will be on show for 2 hours. Decide: keep the Trial 3 set-up ON all the time, or switch it ON only while lifting? Use the record.
questions.a: (a) Two cells give a larger current than one, and a larger current makes a stronger magnetic field, so more clips are lifted. (b) With the same two cells, doubling the turns from 40 to 80 made the electromagnet stronger still (12 clips instead of 7). (c) Left ON for 30 minutes, the cells weakened and supplied less current, so the electromagnet became weaker and lifted only 4 clips. The coil is warm because the current that still flows heats the wire (heating effect of current). (d) Switch it ON only while lifting. Trial 4 shows that just 30 minutes of being left ON cut the clips from 12 to 4; over 2 hours the cells would weaken even more. Short ON periods keep the cells, and so the current and the strength, closer to Trial 3.
s: Part (a): more cells give more current, so a stronger field
Part (b): more turns with the same cells give a stronger magnet
Part (c): cells weakened, less current, weaker magnet; warmth from the heating effect
Part (d): ON only while lifting, as Trial 4 shows long ON weakens the cells

questions.q: A scrap yard is choosing between a crane with an ordinary hook and chains and a crane with a lifting electromagnet. Compare the two on five points: (1) which objects each can lift, (2) how the load is attached, (3) how the load is released, (4) sorting mixed scrap, (5) what happens if the electric supply fails while a load is held. End with which crane suits a yard that handles mostly steel scrap.
questions.a: (1) The hook can lift any object that can be tied to it; the electromagnet lifts only iron and steel objects. (2) The hook needs workers to tie or chain each load; the electromagnet picks up iron and steel directly when switched ON. (3) The hook's load must be untied by hand; the electromagnet releases it when the current is switched OFF and the field disappears. (4) The hook cannot sort; the electromagnet separates iron and steel from non-magnetic scrap in one lift. (5) The hook keeps holding its load; the electromagnet drops its load, because its field exists only while current flows. Conclusion: for mostly steel scrap, the lifting electromagnet is better: faster attaching, instant release and sorting, provided no one works under the load in case of a supply failure.
s: (1) hook: anything tied on; magnet: only iron/steel
(2) hook needs tying; magnet picks up when switched ON
(3) hook untied by hand; magnet releases when switched OFF
(4) only the magnet sorts iron/steel from other scrap
(5) supply failure: magnet drops the load, hook holds it; conclusion for a steel yard

questions.q: Watching Sumana's model, Aakarsh says, 'There must be a hidden magnet inside the battery that pulls the clips up.' Which observation of the model best shows that he is wrong?
questions.a: The clips fall the moment the circuit is opened
o: The clips fall the moment the circuit is opened
The nail inside the coil is made of iron
The wire wound round the nail feels warm
The battery is joined to the coil by two long wires

questions.q:
A model crane magnet made from a coil on an iron nail lifts 5 clips with one cell.
(a) Suggest one change, without replacing the nail, that would let it lift more clips, and say why it works.
(b) A visitor swaps the cell's connections. Will the model still pick up the clips? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Use a battery of two or more cells (a larger current gives a stronger field), or wind more turns of wire on the nail (more turns make a stronger magnet). (b) Yes. Reversing the current only reverses the poles of the electromagnet; it is still a magnet of about the same strength, and iron clips are attracted to it either way.
s: Part (a): more cells or more turns, with the reason
Part (b): yes; only the poles reverse and iron clips are still attracted

questions.q:
At a steel plant, a lifting electromagnet loads steel coils onto railway wagons, one coil per lift, and each lift takes 4 minutes. Next to the coils lie 18 aluminium window frames; aluminium is not a magnetic material.
(a) How long will it take to load 18 steel coils?
(b) Why can the same crane not load the 18 aluminium frames, however strong its current?
questions.a: (a) 18 x 4 = 72 minutes (1 hour 12 minutes). (b) A lifting electromagnet attracts iron and steel objects; aluminium is not a magnetic material, so it is not attracted however strong the magnet is. The frames need a hook or another method.
s: Part (a): 72 minutes
Part (b): aluminium is not magnetic, so the electromagnet cannot attract it

questions.q: A model crane magnet suddenly lifts nothing. When a compass is held right next to its coil with the switch ON, the needle does not deflect at all. What is the most likely cause?
questions.a: No current is flowing through the coil
o: No current is flowing through the coil
Current flows, but the iron core is missing
Current flows, but its poles have reversed
Current flows, but the clips are too heavy

questions.q:
Three students each write one statement after a lesson on the heating effect.
Statement 1: An electric fan works mainly on the heating effect of electric current.
Statement 2: An incandescent lamp and a hair dryer both work on the heating effect of electric current.
Statement 3: Energy lost as heat in long transmission wires is a case where the heating effect is a problem.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: On some evenings the electricity supply in a village near Nashik is weak, and the coil of Jaya's electric stove glows only dull red; on normal evenings the same coil glows bright red. Which idea from the chapter best explains the difference?
questions.a: Less current flows, so less heat is made in the coil
o: Less current flows, so less heat is made in the coil
The coil changes its material when the supply is weak
A weak supply removes all of the resistance of the coil
Less heat is made in the coil whenever more current flows

questions.q: True or False? 'A nichrome wire gets hotter with two cells than with one cell because two cells give the wire more resistance.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Resistance is the opposition that the wire itself offers to the current; adding a second cell does not change the wire. Two cells give a larger current through the same wire, and the heat generated depends on the magnitude of the current, so the wire gets hotter.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the wire is unchanged; two cells give more current, and heat depends on the current

questions.q:
In a supervised lab in Lucknow (room temperature 27 °C), a group stretched different wires, each 10 cm long, between two nails and passed current for 30 seconds. They then read a stick-on thermometer strip on each wire.
Test | Wire | Thickness | Cells | Temperature after 30 s
A | nichrome | 0.3 mm | 1 | 34 °C
B | nichrome | 0.3 mm | 2 | 47 °C
C | copper | 0.3 mm | 1 | 28 °C
D | nichrome | 0.6 mm | 1 | 31 °C
(a) Which two tests show the effect of the current? Give their temperature rises and say what they show.
(b) Which two tests show the effect of the material, and why is that a fair comparison?
(c) What does comparing Test D with Test A show? Why would comparing D with B show nothing clear?
(d) An electric heater has a nichrome element and copper connecting wires, and the same current flows through both. Use the tests to judge whether this is a sensible choice of materials.
questions.a: (a) A and B: rises of 34 - 27 = 7 °C and 47 - 27 = 20 °C. Same wire and time, only the number of cells (the current) changed, so a larger current produces more heat. (b) A and C: same length, same thickness, same cell and same time, only the material changed; nichrome rose 7 °C, copper only 28 - 27 = 1 °C. (c) A and D differ only in thickness: the 0.6 mm nichrome rose 31 - 27 = 4 °C against 7 °C for the 0.3 mm wire, so the thickness of the wire affects the heat produced (here the thicker wire heated less). D and B differ in two things, thickness and number of cells, so any difference could come from either. (d) Sensible. Nichrome offers higher resistance than copper of the same size, so (as A and C show) it turns much more electrical energy into heat, which is wanted in the element. The copper wires heat only slightly, so little energy is wasted in them and they do not overheat.
s: Part (a): A-B, rises 7 °C and 20 °C: more current, more heat
Part (b): A-C, only the material changed (1 °C vs 7 °C)
Part (c): D vs A shows thickness matters (4 °C vs 7 °C); D vs B changes two things
Part (d): sensible: nichrome heats where wanted, copper heats little

questions.q: A shop window shows seven devices: an electric room heater, a ceiling fan, an electric kettle, an electric bell, an electric iron, a loudspeaker and a water heating immersion rod. The number of these that work on the heating effect of electric current is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

Three nichrome wires of the same thickness are tested. P: 10 cm long, 1 cell, 30 s. Q: 10 cm long, 2 cells, 30 s. R: 20 cm long, 1 cell, 60 s. Which pair gives a fair test of whether the current affects the heat produced?
questions.a: P and Q
o: P and Q
P and R
Q and R
None of the pairs

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A thin nichrome wire 20 cm long and one 10 cm long, of the same thickness, joined in turn to the same cell for 30 s, must produce exactly the same heat because they are of the same material.
Reason (R): The heat generated in a wire depends on the material, thickness and length of the wire and on the duration for which the current flows.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
(a) Why is a nichrome wire a good choice for the coil of an electric stove?
(b) Why would nichrome be a poor choice for the long wires that carry current from the switchboard to the stove?
questions.a: (a) Nichrome offers high resistance, so for a given current it converts more electrical energy into heat, which is what a stove needs. (b) In the supply wires the heat is not wanted: high-resistance wires would get hot along their whole length, wasting energy, and could overheat and damage plugs and sockets. (Also accepted: copper offers less resistance than nichrome of the same size, so copper wires waste less energy as heat.)
s: Part (a): high resistance gives more heat for a given current
Part (b): in supply wires the heat is wasted and may cause overheating

questions.q:
Match each case of electric heating in Column I with the best description in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. The nichrome coil of a room heater glowing red | a. Unwanted: energy lost on the way
2. Long wires carrying electricity from a power station | b. Useful: the heat is the purpose
3. A socket overloaded for hours, its plastic softening | c. Placed in the circuit to reduce such incidents
4. A safety device in a household circuit | d. Harmful: may melt parts or start a fire

Neha noticed that the coil of her nail electromagnet got warm. She claims: 'The warmth of my electromagnet's coil and the heat of a kettle's element come from the same effect, even though one is useful and the other is not.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Whenever current flows through a conductor, it faces resistance, and some electrical energy is converted into heat: this is the heating effect of electric current. In the kettle's heating element this heat is the purpose. In the electromagnet's coil the same effect only wastes some of the cell's energy as heat, since the coil is meant to act as a magnet.
s: Verdict: yes, she is right
Current through any conductor meets resistance and produces heat (heating effect)
Useful in the kettle element, a waste in the electromagnet coil

questions.q: Kiran uses the same electric iron, on the same setting, twice: once for 2 minutes and once for 10 minutes. In which case does its element produce more heat in total, and why?
questions.a: 10 minutes, as heat depends on how long current flows
o: 10 minutes, as heat depends on how long current flows
2 minutes, as an element is hottest when first switched on
Same in both, as the current through it is the same
Same in both, as the material of its element is unchanged

questions.q:
A student writes: 'The heating effect of electric current is just a waste of electricity.' Here are six cases:
(i) the element of a toaster glowing red; (ii) the coil of a crane's lifting electromagnet getting warm; (iii) a water heating immersion rod warming a bucket of water; (iv) energy lost along the long wires from a power station; (v) the plastic of an overloaded socket softening after a heater runs all evening; (vi) the filament of an incandescent lamp.
Evaluate the statement in five points: choose two cases where the heat is useful, and two where it is a problem; for each problem case, name one factor from the chapter (material, current or duration) whose change would reduce the heat, and how; then give your judgement.
questions.a: (1) Useful: any two of (i), (iii) and (vi), for example the toaster element and the immersion rod, where producing heat (or the glow of a heated filament) is the purpose of the device. (2) The second useful case, with the same reason. (3) Problem (iv): energy is lost as heat in transmission wires; using a material of lower resistance (copper rather than nichrome, as copper heats far less for the same size and current) reduces the heat. (4) Problem (v): overheating can melt plastic parts of plugs and sockets or start a fire; running the heater for a shorter duration, or drawing less current through that socket, reduces the heat. (Case (ii) is also a waste, reduced by keeping the magnet switched ON only while lifting.) (5) Judgement: the statement is only partly true. The effect wastes energy or is dangerous in wires and overloaded sockets, but in heating appliances and lamps it is exactly what is wanted.
s: First useful case, with heat as the purpose
Second useful case
First problem case with a factor and its direction (e.g. lower-resistance material for wires)
Second problem case with a factor and its direction (e.g. shorter duration or less current)
Judgement: only partly true, with reason

questions.q:
In a nichrome-wire activity, students are told: 'Move the switch to OFF, then touch the wire only for a moment; do not hold it.'
(a) Why must the wire not be held?
(b) A classmate says, 'The wire is warm only because the cardboard under it passes on heat from the cell.' Correct him.
questions.a: (a) The current has heated the wire (heating effect), and holding a hot wire for an extended period can cause injury such as a burn. (b) The heat is produced in the wire itself: as current flows through the nichrome, it faces resistance, and this converts some of the electrical energy into heat in the wire. The cardboard only holds the nails.
s: Part (a): the wire is heated by the current; holding it can injure
Part (b): heat is produced in the wire itself by its resistance to the current

questions.q:
In Mr Desai's tailoring shop in Surat, an electric iron runs from an old extension board. Explain each of these observations using the heating effect of electric current.
(i) The iron's base gets hot within minutes of being switched on.
(ii) When a mechanic opened a faulty iron, the coil inside had been glowing red.
(iii) The iron's copper cord feels only slightly warm.
(iv) After a long working day, the plastic around one socket of the extension board had softened.
(v) The electrician says the shop's household circuit has a safety device for exactly such cases.
questions.a: (i) The iron has a heating element: current flowing through it faces resistance, and some electrical energy is converted into heat that warms the base. (ii) The heating element is a coil of wire; in some appliances it can get hot enough to glow red. (iii) The copper cord also carries the current, but copper offers much less resistance than the element's wire, so very little heat is produced in it. (iv) Running for many hours overheated the socket, and overheating can damage plugs and sockets by melting their plastic parts. (v) Overheating can even lead to fires, so household circuits include safety devices to minimise such incidents.
s: (i) heating element: resistance converts electrical energy into heat
(ii) the element is a coil that can glow red hot
(iii) copper cord has low resistance, so little heat
(iv) overheating melts plastic parts of sockets
(v) safety devices minimise overheating incidents such as fires

questions.q:
Under a teacher's supervision, a school in Jaipur is making a hot-wire cutter for a Class 6 craft period: a nichrome wire stretched between two posts, which must get hot enough to melt through thermocol. A trial gave:
Power | Time for one cut | ON-time before the cells are too weak to cut
1 cell | 12 s | about 40 minutes
battery of 2 cells | 4 s | about 25 minutes
In the 60-minute period, 30 students will make 3 cuts each, and the teacher wants all the cutting done within 15 minutes of ON-time.
(a) Using the chapter, explain why the wire gets hot enough to melt thermocol at all.
(b) Find the total ON-time needed for all the cuts with each power choice. Which choice meets the 15-minute limit?
(c) A student suggests keeping the switch ON for the whole 60-minute period 'so the wire is always ready'. Use the table to show what would happen with each choice.
(d) Decide the power choice and the switching plan, and give one safety instruction with its reason.
questions.a: (a) When current flows through the nichrome wire, it faces resistance, which is high for nichrome; this converts some of the electrical energy into heat (the heating effect of electric current), so the wire gets hot. (b) 30 x 3 = 90 cuts. One cell: 90 x 12 = 1,080 s = 18 minutes, which is over the limit. Two cells: 90 x 4 = 360 s = 6 minutes, within the limit. (c) Both would fail before the period ends: one cell becomes too weak after about 40 minutes and the two-cell battery after about 25 minutes, so cutting would stop part-way through the 60 minutes. (d) Use the battery of two cells, switched ON only while each cut is made: that needs only 6 of its 25 minutes, and it is the only choice that meets the 15-minute limit. Safety: never touch the wire, even just after switching OFF, because the current has heated it and touching it can cause injury.
s: Part (a): resistance of nichrome converts electrical energy to heat
Part (b): 18 min (1 cell, fails) vs 6 min (2 cells, meets the limit)
Part (c): kept ON, both fail (40 min and 25 min are under 60 min)
Part (d): 2 cells, ON only during cuts (6 of 25 min); do not touch the hot wire

questions.q: Differentiate between an incandescent lamp and an electric room heater: state what they have in common and how they differ in the use they make of the heating effect.
questions.a: Common: both contain a wire (filament or heating element) that is heated by the electric current passing through it. Differ: in the lamp the filament is heated so much that it glows and gives light, which is its purpose; in the room heater the heat itself is the purpose.
s: Common: a wire heated by the current
Differ: lamp uses the heat to glow and give light; heater uses the heat itself

questions.q:
Shalini connects two nichrome wires, one after the other, to the same cell for 30 seconds each. Wire 2 becomes noticeably hotter than Wire 1.
(a) Apart from the material, current and time (all kept the same), name two features of the wires that could differ and affect the heat produced.
(b) Why can she not tell from this test alone which of those features caused the difference?
questions.a: (a) The thickness of the wire and the length of the wire; the heat generated depends on both, as well as on the material, the current and the duration. (b) She does not know whether the wires differ in thickness, in length, or in both. To find out which matters, she must change only one feature at a time and keep everything else the same.
s: Part (a): thickness and length of the wire
Part (b): both may differ, so only one feature must be changed at a time

questions.q: While making an electromagnet with a copper wire coiled on a nail, Om finds that the ends of the wire have become warm. Which statement explains this?
questions.a: Current in any conductor meets resistance and makes heat
o: Current in any conductor meets resistance and makes heat
The nail's magnetism is passing heat into the copper wire
Only nichrome heats up, so his wire must be nichrome
The cell has turned into a heating element for the coil

questions.q: A lab notebook ends with: 'So the heat generated in the wire depends on the magnitude of the electric current.' Describe the comparison that leads to exactly this conclusion: what was changed, what was kept the same, and what was observed.
questions.a: Changed: the current, by using one cell in the first trial and a battery of two cells in the second. Kept the same: the wire (same nichrome wire, same material, thickness and length) and the duration, say 30 seconds each. Observed: the wire became hotter with two cells than with one cell, so a larger current produced more heat.
s: Changed: number of cells (current)
Kept the same: wire material, thickness, length and duration
Observed: hotter with two cells

questions.q:
Electricity reaches a town in Odisha through long wires from a distant power station.
(a) Which effect of current causes some energy to be lost along these wires, and in what form is it lost?
(b) The chapter calls this effect a problem in these wires but calls it useful in an electric kettle. Explain why the same effect is judged differently.
questions.a: (a) The heating effect of electric current: the wires offer some resistance, so part of the electrical energy is converted into heat and lost along the way. (b) In the kettle, heat is what the appliance is meant to produce, so the effect is useful. In supply wires the aim is only to carry electrical energy to the town, so any heat produced there is wasted energy.
s: Part (a): heating effect; energy lost as heat
Part (b): heat is the purpose in the kettle but a waste in supply wires

questions.q: Explain, in three linked steps, how energy stored in an electric cell ends up as heat in a nichrome wire connected across it.
questions.a: (1) Inside the cell a chemical reaction produces electricity, so when the circuit is closed an electric current flows through the wire. (2) As the current flows through the nichrome, it faces opposition, that is resistance, which is high for nichrome. (3) This resistance causes some of the electrical energy to be converted into heat energy, so the wire gets heated (heating effect of electric current).
s: Chemical reaction in the cell drives a current through the wire
The current faces resistance, high in nichrome
Resistance converts electrical energy into heat in the wire

questions.q: Ritu says, 'Our electric kettle cannot be using the heating effect, because unlike our room heater I never see anything inside it glowing red.' Which reply is best?
questions.a: Its heating element is heated; it is just hidden
o: Its heating element is heated; it is just hidden
She is right; a kettle works on the magnetic effect
She is right; its water is heated by the warm cord
Its element is heated only when the kettle is empty

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A lemon with a copper wire and an iron nail pushed into it, a little apart, can work as an electric cell.
Reason (R): Two electrodes of different metals react chemically with an electrolyte to produce electricity, and lemon juice can act as the electrolyte.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A teacher in Mysuru dips an iron nail and a copper wire, a little apart, into salt solution in a glass beaker and connects them through a small lamp, which glows.
(a) Name the parts of this cell that the nail, the wire and the salt solution are, and say what is required of the nail and the wire.
(b) She then replaces the iron nail with a second copper wire, and the lamp does not glow. Explain.
questions.a: (a) The iron nail and the copper wire are the electrodes and the salt solution is the electrolyte; the two electrodes must be made of different metals (different materials). (b) With two copper wires, the electrodes are no longer of different materials, so the set-up is not a Voltaic cell and no electricity is produced; the lamp stays dark.
s: Part (a): nail and wire = electrodes, salt solution = electrolyte; electrodes must be different metals
Part (b): two copper wires are not different materials, so no electricity is produced

questions.q: True or False? 'In a lemon cell, the lemon itself makes the electricity; the copper wire and iron nail only collect it.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The electricity is produced by a chemical reaction between the two metal electrodes (the copper wire and the iron nail) and the electrolyte (the lemon juice). The lemon juice acts as the electrolyte that conducts electricity between them; the metals are an essential part of the reaction, not just collectors.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a chemical reaction between the two different metal electrodes and the electrolyte produces the electricity

questions.q:
A group writes three statements about the lemon cell chain they built, in which each lemon's iron nail is joined by a wire to the next lemon's copper wire.
Statement 1: In each lemon, the copper wire and the iron nail are the electrodes.
Statement 2: The lemon juice in each lemon acts as an electrode of the cell.
Statement 3: The LED is connected between the iron nail of the first lemon and the iron nail of the last lemon.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Diya pushes a copper wire into one lemon and an iron nail into a second lemon kept beside it, and connects an LED between the copper wire and the nail. The LED stays dark whichever way round it is joined. What is wrong?
questions.a: The two electrodes are in different lemons, so no juice joins them; both must dip into the same lemon
o: The two electrodes are in different lemons, so no juice joins them; both must dip into the same lemon
Two lemons are too few to make any LED glow at all
The copper wire should be replaced by a second iron nail
The nail and the copper wire must touch each other inside

questions.q: A student lists everything in her working chain of lemon cells: 5 lemons, 5 copper wires, 5 iron nails, 1 LED and 6 connecting wires. The number of electrodes in her chain is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

For a science fair in Ranchi, Class 8 tested five set-ups. Each is a chain of 5 cells joined the same way, with an LED across its ends connected the right way round unless noted.
Set-up | Electrodes in each cell | Liquid in each cell | LED
P | copper wire + iron nail | lemon juice | glows
Q | copper wire + copper wire | lemon juice | dark
R | copper wire + iron nail | salt solution | glows
S | copper wire + iron nail | pure distilled water | dark
T | copper wire + iron nail | lemon juice, LED connected the other way | dark
(a) Why does Q fail although it has the same liquid as P?
(b) What does comparing R and S show about the liquid?
(c) T has working cells. Explain why its LED is dark and how to fix it.
(d) On day 2 of the fair, P's LED is very dim, and the team must decide whether to replace P's lemons or P's LED. They have time for one test only: moving P's LED onto chain R. Explain how this one test decides, giving the conclusion for each possible result.
questions.a: (a) A Voltaic cell needs two electrodes of different metals; Q's two copper wires are the same metal, so no electricity is produced. (b) The liquid must be an electrolyte, usually a weak acid or a salt solution. Salt solution works as the electrolyte; pure distilled water, which is neither, does not, so the LED stays dark. (c) Current passes through an LED only when its longer (positive) leg is joined to the positive terminal and its shorter leg to the negative terminal. T's LED is the wrong way round; reversing its connections will make it glow. (d) Chain R is working, so it is a fair check of the LED. If P's LED glows brightly on R, the LED is fine and the fault is in P's cells: their chemicals are being used up and the cells are going 'dead', so replace the lemons. If P's LED is still dim (or dark) on R, the LED is the faulty part, so replace the LED.
s: Part (a): electrodes must be different metals
Part (b): salt solution is an electrolyte; pure water is not
Part (c): LED reversed; current passes only with longer leg to positive; swap its connections
Part (d): bright on R means P's cells are used up (replace lemons); dim on R means the LED is faulty

questions.q: Lemon cells glow an LED at a stall. Mira pulls the iron nail out of the third lemon in the chain of six. What happens to the LED?
questions.a: It goes off, as the chain is now broken
o: It goes off, as the chain is now broken
It stays on, as five lemons still work
