It stays on, but only the third lemon dies

questions.q: A group finds that one lemon cell on its own does not light their LED, but five lemon cells joined in a chain do. Kiran concludes: 'So a single lemon with a copper wire and an iron nail is not an electric cell at all.' Is his conclusion right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Wrong. A single lemon with a copper wire and an iron nail has everything a Voltaic cell needs: two electrodes of different metals and an electrolyte (lemon juice), between which a chemical reaction produces electricity. So it is a cell. The observation only shows that one lemon cell did not produce enough to light this LED, while the chain of five cells did.
s: Verdict: wrong
A single lemon has two different metal electrodes and an electrolyte, so it is a cell
The observation shows only that one cell was not enough for the LED

questions.q: Viren pushes a copper wire and an iron nail, a little apart, into a potato and joins an LED the right way round across them; it glows faintly. Which part of this potato cell plays the role of the electrolyte?
questions.a: The juice inside the potato
o: The juice inside the potato
The copper wire, as it carries current
The iron nail, as it reacts in the potato
The connecting wires to the LED

questions.q:
At a camp in Coorg, a group has copper wires, iron nails and cups but no lemons.
(a) Suggest a liquid they could make from camp supplies to fill the cups instead of lemon juice.
(b) Name the part of the cell this liquid becomes and the job it does there.
questions.a: (a) A salt solution, made by dissolving common salt in water. (b) It becomes the electrolyte: the copper and iron electrodes react chemically with it to produce electricity, and it conducts electricity between the two electrodes.
s: Part (a): salt solution
Part (b): electrolyte, reacts with the electrodes and conducts between them

questions.q:
At a Class 8 science stall, five set-ups are each connected to an LED joined the right way round. For each, decide whether it can work as an electric cell, and if not, name the part of a Voltaic cell that is missing or wrong.
(1) A copper wire and an iron nail pushed a little apart into a juicy lemon.
(2) Two iron nails dipped a little apart in a cup of salt solution.
(3) A copper wire and an iron nail standing in an empty, dry glass.
(4) A copper wire and an iron nail dipped a little apart in a cup of vinegar, a weak acid.
(5) A copper wire and an iron nail in a jar of salt solution that lit the LED for a week but now gives nothing, though every joint is firm and the LED works on another cell.
questions.a: (1) Works: two electrodes of different metals (copper and iron) with lemon juice as the electrolyte. (2) Does not work: the two electrodes are of the same metal; a Voltaic cell needs electrodes of different materials. (3) Does not work: there is no electrolyte for the electrodes to react with. (4) Works: different metals, and the electrolyte is a weak acid, as a Voltaic cell's electrolyte usually is. (5) No longer works: the cell is 'dead'; over time the chemicals taking part in the reaction get used up and it cannot supply any more electricity.
s: (1) works: different metals plus lemon-juice electrolyte
(2) fails: electrodes of the same metal
(3) fails: no electrolyte
(4) works: weak acid is an electrolyte
(5) dead: its chemicals are used up

questions.q: An online advert says: 'Our lemon-cell kit never goes dead. Set it up once and your LED will glow forever on the same lemons.' Show, using the chapter, that this claim cannot be true.
questions.a: A lemon cell produces electricity by a chemical reaction between its electrodes and the lemon juice. As the cell works, the chemicals taking part in this reaction get used up. Once they are used up, the cell stops working: it is then 'dead' and cannot supply any more electricity. So the LED cannot glow forever on the same lemons; the lemons (and in time the electrodes) must be replaced.
s: Electricity comes from a chemical reaction
The chemicals get used up as the cell works
So the cell goes dead and the LED cannot glow forever

questions.q:
Anjali in Thane joined four lemon cells, A, B, C and D, each holding one copper wire and one iron nail. Her teacher's rule card says: 'Join the iron nail of each lemon to the copper wire of the next lemon. Connect the LED between the copper wire of the first lemon and the iron nail of the last lemon. The copper wire is the positive terminal.' Anjali's record:
Joint 1: copper wire of A to copper wire of B
Joint 2: iron nail of B to copper wire of C
Joint 3: iron nail of C to iron nail of D
LED: between the copper wire of A and the copper wire of D
(a) Which joints break the rule? Correct them.
(b) After correcting the joints, where should the LED's two ends go, and which leg goes to A's copper wire? Why?
(c) Before she fixed anything, her friend said, 'The joints don't matter; each lemon is a cell anyway.' Which half of this is right, and which half is wrong?
(d) After all the fixes, the LED stays dark whichever way round it is joined, but it glows when tried on a fresh dry cell. Decide what Anjali should replace, and explain using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Joint 1 breaks the rule: it should join the iron nail of A to the copper wire of B. Joint 3 breaks it: it should join the iron nail of C to the copper wire of D. (Joint 2 is correct.) (b) Between the copper wire of A and the iron nail of D. The longer (positive) leg goes to A's copper wire, the positive terminal, because current passes through an LED only when its longer leg is joined to the positive terminal and its shorter leg to the negative terminal. (c) Right: each lemon with a copper wire and an iron nail is a cell (two different metal electrodes in an electrolyte). Wrong: the joints do matter; the cells must be joined as the rule says for the chain to light the LED. (d) Replace the lemons (the cells). The dry-cell test shows the LED works, so the fault is in the lemon cells: over time their chemicals get used up and the cells stop working ('dead'), so they cannot supply electricity.
s: Part (a): Joints 1 and 3 break the rule, with corrections
Part (b): LED from A's copper to D's nail; longer leg to A's copper (positive)
Part (c): each lemon is a cell (right), but the joining matters (wrong)
Part (d): replace the lemons; the LED works, so the cells are used up

questions.q: A chain of lemon cells has lit an LED at a stall for four days. Which observation best shows that the chemicals in the cells are getting used up?
questions.a: The LED grows dimmer each day, though no joint has changed
o: The LED grows dimmer each day, though no joint has changed
The LED glows only when its longer leg goes to the copper wire
The LED goes off when one nail is pulled out of a lemon
The LED glows again when its two legs are joined the right way

questions.q: Mansi wants to find out whether salt solution works as well as lemon juice as the electrolyte in a home-made cell chain. She has copper wires, iron nails, cups, lemons, salt, water, connecting wires and one LED. Her rule card says: 'Join the iron nail of each cell to the copper wire of the next; connect the LED between the first copper wire and the last iron nail.' Plan her investigation in five points: (1) the one thing she changes, (2) two things she keeps the same and why, (3) how each cell must be set up, (4) what she observes, and (5) what she can conclude if the LED glows equally well with both.
questions.a: (1) Change only the electrolyte: one chain uses lemon juice (lemons), the other uses salt solution in cups. (2) Keep the same: the electrode metals (copper wire and iron nail in every cell), the number of cells in each chain, and the same LED joined the same way; if any of these changed too, she could not tell what caused a difference. (3) In each cell, a copper wire and an iron nail are partly dipped in the electrolyte, a little apart, because a cell needs two electrodes of different metals in an electrolyte. (4) Whether the LED glows, and how brightly, for each chain. (5) Both lemon juice and salt solution act as electrolytes: with the electrodes they produce electricity by a chemical reaction, so salt solution can be used instead of lemon juice.
s: (1) changes only the electrolyte
(2) keeps electrodes, number of cells and LED the same, with the fair-test reason
(3) two different metal electrodes partly dipped, apart, in the electrolyte
(4) observes whether and how brightly the LED glows
(5) both liquids act as electrolytes

questions.q:
Two lemon chains are built in exactly the same way. Chain X uses juicy lemons; chain Y uses lemons that have dried out completely. Only X lights the LED.
(a) Which part of a Voltaic cell is missing in chain Y? Explain.
(b) A student sprinkles dry salt crystals on Y's lemons and says it will now work as salt is an electrolyte. Why is this not what the chapter means?
questions.a: (a) The electrolyte. In a lemon cell the electrolyte is the lemon juice, which helps conduct electricity between the electrodes and reacts with them; dried-out lemons have no juice, so no electricity is produced. (b) The chapter's electrolyte is a salt solution (salt dissolved in a liquid), not dry salt; a Voltaic cell's electrolyte is a liquid, usually a weak acid or salt solution, in which the electrodes are dipped.
s: Part (a): the electrolyte (lemon juice) is missing
Part (b): the electrolyte must be a salt solution (a liquid), not dry crystals

questions.q:
Kiran's chain of 5 lemon cells, joined correctly, makes an LED glow only dimly, even though the lemons are fresh and the LED is joined the right way round.
(a) Suggest one change to the cells that would make a larger current flow through the LED (a larger current makes an LED glow more brightly).
(b) Give the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Add more lemon cells to the chain (for example 6 or more), joined the same way, iron nail of one to copper wire of the next. (b) A battery with more cells gives a larger current than one with fewer cells, so more current passes through the LED.
s: Part (a): add more lemon cells, joined the same way
Part (b): more cells give a larger current

questions.q: Design a Voltaic cell using only things found in an Indian kitchen or toolbox, in which the electrolyte is a salt solution. Name what you would use for each of the three parts of the cell and give the reason each choice fits.
questions.a: Electrodes: an iron nail and a copper wire (for example from an old electric cord), because the two electrodes must be rods of different metals. Electrolyte: common salt dissolved in water, because the electrolyte is usually a weak acid or salt solution and it must conduct electricity between the electrodes. Container: a glass tumbler or plastic cup, because a Voltaic cell holds its electrolyte in a glass or plastic container, with the two electrodes partly dipped in it and kept apart.
s: Electrodes: two different metals, e.g. iron nail and copper wire
Electrolyte: salt solution, with its role
Container: glass or plastic, electrodes partly dipped and apart

questions.q: Rehan wants a liquid electrolyte for a cell with a copper wire and an iron nail. Which of these kitchen items should he choose?
questions.a: Vinegar, which is a weak acid

Cooking oil, which is a liquid
Distilled water, as it is purest

questions.q: A Voltaic cell with a zinc rod and a copper rod in dilute acid lights a bulb. A student lifts both rods right out of the acid, keeping the wires connected. What happens?
questions.a: The bulb goes off; the rods must dip in the electrolyte
o: The bulb goes off; the rods must dip in the electrolyte
The bulb stays on; the rods still hold their electricity
The bulb glows brighter; the acid was blocking current
The bulb stays on until the wet rods dry completely

questions.q: A torch dry cell, a lemon cell and a mobile-phone battery look very different. What do all three have in common?
questions.a: Each makes current by chemical reactions inside it
o: Each makes current by chemical reactions inside it
Each has a liquid electrolyte, like a Voltaic cell
Each can be recharged and reused many times over
Each has a zinc container as its negative terminal

questions.q:
A student describes the parts of a dry cell in her own words. Match each description in Column I with the part in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. The outer case, which is the negative terminal | a. Metal cap over the carbon rod
2. The part at the top centre, which is the positive terminal | b. Zinc container
3. The layer that is moist but not a liquid | c. Paste-like electrolyte
4. The rod at the centre, under the positive terminal | d. Carbon rod
True or False? 'Since a dry cell has no liquid inside, it works without any electrolyte, unlike a Voltaic cell.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. A dry cell does have an electrolyte: it is a thick, moist paste surrounding the carbon rod, not a liquid. It is called 'dry' only because its electrolyte is not a liquid as in a Voltaic cell.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: its electrolyte is a thick moist paste around the carbon rod; 'dry' means not liquid

questions.q:
Raju's grandmother in Madurai uses a basic phone with a rechargeable battery, about 5 hours of use every day. The family noted how many hours of use one full charge gave.
Age of battery | Hours of use per full charge
New | 30
1 year | 25
2 years | 20
3 years | 15
Every week she spends 2 days at the family farm, where there is no electricity, so one full charge must last her at least 2 days. A new battery costs Rs 600.
(a) The battery is still recharged fully every time. Explain, using the chapter, why each charge now gives fewer hours.
(b) How many days does one charge last now? If the hours keep falling by the same amount each year, how many days will a charge last at 4 years and at 5 years?
(c) Is this battery 'dead' like a used-up dry cell? Explain.
(d) Raju's cousin says, 'Buy a new battery now; it is worth it.' Decide whether to buy now, using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Rechargeable batteries do not last forever: after being charged and used many times, they slowly wear out, so each full charge gives fewer hours of use. (b) Now (3 years): 15 / 5 = 3 days. The hours fall by 5 each year, so at 4 years 10 hours = 2 days, and at 5 years 5 hours = 1 day. (c) No. A used-up dry cell cannot supply any more electricity and has to be disposed of. This battery still works for 15 hours on every charge and can still be recharged and reused; it has only partly worn out. (d) Not yet. Today a charge lasts 3 days, more than the 2 days she needs at the farm, so the Rs 600 is not needed now. At about 4 years it will just meet the 2-day need, and by 5 years (1 day) it will fail, so the family should plan to buy a new battery at around the 4-year mark.
s: Part (a): rechargeable batteries slowly wear out after many charges and uses
Part (b): 3 days now; 2 days at 4 years; 1 day at 5 years
Part (c): not dead: it still works and can be recharged, unlike a used-up dry cell
Part (d): not yet; 3 days > 2 days needed; buy around 4 years

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For everyday use in a torch, a dry cell is more convenient than a Voltaic cell made of two rods in a glass container of liquid.
Reason (R): The zinc container of a dry cell acts as its negative terminal.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Three statements about cells and batteries are given.
Statement 1: Dry cells and rechargeable batteries both generate electric current because of chemical reactions inside them.
Statement 2: Rechargeable batteries come in many sizes, from small ones in watches and phones to big ones that run inverters or drive electric vehicles.
Statement 3: In a dry cell, the zinc container acts as the positive terminal.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
A lemon cell has a copper wire (positive terminal), an iron nail (negative terminal) and lemon juice.
(a) Which part of a dry cell does the job of the lemon juice, and which two parts act as its positive and negative terminals in place of the copper wire and the iron nail?
(b) A lemon cell needs no separate container because the lemon holds the juice. Which part of a dry cell holds its electrolyte and is also one of its terminals?
questions.a: (a) The thick, moist paste is the electrolyte, doing the job of the lemon juice. The carbon rod with its metal cap is the positive terminal (like the copper wire), and the zinc container is the negative terminal (like the iron nail). (b) The zinc container: it holds the paste-like electrolyte around the carbon rod and also acts as the negative terminal.
s: Part (a): paste = electrolyte; carbon rod with cap = positive; zinc container = negative
Part (b): the zinc container holds the paste and is the negative terminal

questions.q: When it was new, Meena's mobile phone needed charging once a day. Two years later, with the same use, it needs charging twice a day. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: Its rechargeable battery has slowly worn out
o: Its rechargeable battery has slowly worn out
Its battery has changed into a single-use cell
Its battery now has a liquid in place of a paste
Its battery was a dry cell from the beginning

questions.q: Arnav claims: 'Rechargeable batteries are better than dry cells because they can be used again and again, so they last forever and never become waste.' Is his claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused multiple times, unlike single-use dry cells, which prevents wastage and saves money over time. But they do not last forever: after being charged and used many times they slowly wear out, so in the end they too have to be replaced.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: reused many times, so less wastage and money saved
Wrong part: they wear out after many charges, so they do not last forever

questions.q: Evaluate the claim 'The dry cell is simply a better cell than the Voltaic cell.' Compare the two on four points, (1) how each produces electricity, (2) the form of the electrolyte, (3) what acts as the two terminals, and (4) how suitable each is for everyday use, and then (5) give your judgement, saying in what sense the claim is right and in what sense it goes too far.
questions.a: (1) Both produce electricity by chemical reactions inside them, between the electrodes and the electrolyte; in this they are the same. (2) A Voltaic cell has a liquid electrolyte (usually a weak acid or salt solution) in a glass or plastic container; a dry cell has a thick, moist paste. (3) A Voltaic cell has two metal rods of different materials partly dipped in the liquid; a dry cell has a zinc container (negative terminal) and a carbon rod with a metal cap (positive terminal). (4) Voltaic cells are not convenient for everyday use, while dry cells are one of the most widely used electric cells today. (5) The claim is right for everyday use, where the paste-filled dry cell is far more convenient. It goes too far as a general claim: both work on the same principle, the Voltaic cell was the important earlier discovery, and a dry cell is single-use, so once used up it has to be disposed of.
s: (1) both by chemical reactions: same principle
(2) liquid electrolyte vs thick moist paste
(3) two different metal rods vs zinc container (-) and carbon rod with cap (+)
(4) Voltaic not convenient; dry cells widely used
(5) judgement: right for everyday use, too far overall (same principle, earlier discovery, single-use)

questions.q: A family's TV remote and wall clock together use 4 single-use dry cells, and all 4 are replaced every 3 months. Over 2 years, the family throws away ___ dry cells. (Write the number in digits.)

Ravi's toy crane magnet lifts 3 clips with one dry cell and 7 clips with a battery of two dry cells.
(a) Explain the difference.
(b) After a week of play the two-cell battery lifts only 1 clip, though every joint is firm and the coil is unchanged. What has happened inside the dry cells, and what must be done with them?
questions.a: (a) A battery with more cells gives a larger current than a single cell, and a larger current makes a stronger magnet, so more clips are lifted. (b) The chemicals inside the dry cells are getting used up, so they supply less and less current. Dry cells are single-use: once used up they cannot be recharged and have to be disposed of and replaced.
s: Part (a): two cells give a larger current, so a stronger magnet
Part (b): chemicals used up; single-use, so disposed of and replaced

questions.q:
Sneha in Bhubaneswar wrote these revision notes after studying a diagram of a dry cell:
Note 1: The outer zinc container is the positive terminal.
Note 2: The carbon rod at the centre, with its metal cap, is the negative terminal.
Note 3: The electrolyte inside is a dry powder, which is why it is called a dry cell.
Note 4: In a torch, current flows out of the zinc container, through the bulb, and back into the metal cap.
(a) Notes 1 and 2 contain the same kind of mistake. Find it and correct both notes.
(b) Correct Note 3, and explain why the cell is still called 'dry'.
(c) After correcting Notes 1 and 2, decide whether Note 4 is right. If not, rewrite it and give the rule you used.
questions.a: (a) The terminals are swapped. Note 1: the zinc container is the negative terminal. Note 2: the carbon rod with its metal cap is the positive terminal. (b) The electrolyte is a thick, moist paste around the carbon rod, not a dry powder. It is called 'dry' because the electrolyte is not a liquid. (c) Note 4 is wrong, because it follows from her swapped terminals. When a circuit is connected, current flows from the positive terminal through the circuit to the negative terminal. So: current flows out of the metal cap (positive), through the bulb, and back into the zinc container (negative).
s: Part (a): terminals swapped: zinc is negative, carbon rod with cap is positive
Part (b): moist paste, not powder; called dry because it is not a liquid
Part (c): wrong; current flows from the metal cap (positive) through the bulb to the zinc container (negative)

questions.q: A school in Indore uses 60 single-use dry cells a month in clocks, torches and lab kits, at Rs 20 each. It could instead buy 60 rechargeable cells at Rs 100 each plus chargers costing Rs 1,500 (ignore the cost of electricity for charging). The seller says the rechargeable cells will last 2 years. Work out (a) the cost of dry cells over 2 years, (b) the cost of the rechargeable set and the saving, (c) using the chapter, explain why the rechargeable cells cannot be expected to last for ever, and recompute the saving over 2 years if they wear out after only 1 year and a second set of 60 cells is bought (the chargers are kept), (d) how many cells would be thrown away in 2 years in each of the three cases, and (e) judge the statement 'Rechargeable cells are good for the pocket and the planet'.
questions.a: (a) 60 x 20 = Rs 1,200 a month; over 24 months, 1,200 x 24 = Rs 28,800. (b) 60 x 100 + 1,500 = Rs 7,500, a saving of 28,800 - 7,500 = Rs 21,300. (c) Rechargeable batteries do not last forever: after being charged and used many times they slowly wear out. If they last only 1 year: 2 x 6,000 + 1,500 = Rs 13,500, so the saving falls to 28,800 - 13,500 = Rs 15,300. (d) Dry cells: 60 x 24 = 1,440; rechargeable lasting 2 years: 60; rechargeable lasting 1 year: 120. (e) The statement is supported even in the worse case: the school still saves Rs 15,300 and throws away 120 cells instead of 1,440, because rechargeable cells are recharged and reused many times, which saves money over time and prevents wastage. Its limit is that they wear out, so the saving depends on how long they last, and the first purchase costs more than a month of dry cells.
s: (a) Rs 28,800 for dry cells
(b) Rs 7,500 and a saving of Rs 21,300
(c) they wear out after many charges; 1-year life: Rs 13,500, saving Rs 15,300
(d) 1,440 against 60 (or 120)
(e) judgement: supported, with the limit that they wear out

questions.q: Trace the 'life story' of a dry cell in a torch in four stages: (1) how it produces current when the torch is switched on, (2) which of its parts the current leaves from and returns to, (3) what is happening inside as the weeks of use pass, and (4) what must be done with it at the end, and why.
questions.a: (1) Chemical reactions taking place inside the cell generate an electric current when the circuit is closed. (2) The current flows from the positive terminal, the metal cap on the carbon rod, through the torch's bulb and back to the negative terminal, the zinc container. (3) As it is used, the chemicals inside get used up, and the cell supplies less until it stops working. (4) Once its chemicals are used up it is 'dead' and cannot supply any more electricity; it is a single-use cell, so it has to be disposed of and replaced with a new one.
s: (1) chemical reactions inside generate the current
(2) out from the metal cap (positive), back to the zinc container (negative)
(3) the chemicals get used up over time
(4) dead when the chemicals are used up; single-use, so disposed of and replaced

Rima's torch holds two dry cells, one above the other, with the bulb's contact at the top. The torch's bottom spring presses on the zinc base of the lower cell, and the instruction card says: 'Cells in a battery are joined positive terminal to negative terminal.'
(a) Which part of the lower cell must touch which part of the upper cell?
(b) Which part of the upper cell then touches the bulb's contact, and is it positive or negative?
questions.a: (a) The metal cap on the carbon rod of the lower cell (its positive terminal) must touch the zinc base of the upper cell's container (its negative terminal). (b) The metal cap of the upper cell, which is a positive terminal, touches the bulb's contact.
s: Part (a): metal cap (positive) of the lower cell touches the zinc container (negative) of the upper cell
Part (b): the upper cell's metal cap, positive

questions.q:
A pair of rechargeable AA batteries costs Rs 360, and a pair of single-use AA dry cells costs Rs 40.
(a) How many pairs of dry cells cost the same as one pair of rechargeable batteries (ignore charging costs)?
(b) If the rechargeable pair is recharged and reused far more times than that, give the two benefits the chapter names for choosing it.
questions.a: (a) 360 / 40 = 9 pairs. (b) It saves money over time (every reuse beyond the ninth costs nothing extra in cells), and it prevents wastage, since far fewer cells are thrown away.
s: Part (a): 9 pairs
Part (b): saves money over time and prevents wastage

questions.q: Priya's torch cells have run out. Her friend claims: 'Just put those dry cells on your phone charger overnight and they will be as good as new.' Is the claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter, and say what Priya should do.
questions.a: Wrong. A dry cell is a single-use cell: once it is used up, it cannot be recharged and has to be disposed of. Only rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused. Priya should dispose of the used dry cells and buy new ones, or switch to rechargeable batteries for her torch so that next time she can recharge them.
s: Verdict: wrong
Dry cells are single-use and cannot be recharged
What to do: dispose of them and buy new ones, or switch to rechargeable batteries

questions.q: A student's diagram shows a 'dry cell' whose two terminals are both made of zinc: a zinc container and a zinc rod at the centre, with a paste between them. Show that this cannot be a working cell.
questions.a: A cell produces electricity by a chemical reaction between two electrodes and an electrolyte, and the two electrodes must be made of different materials (as in a Voltaic cell). In the diagram both terminals are zinc, the same material, so no electricity would be produced even though a paste is present. A real dry cell has a zinc container as the negative terminal and a carbon rod with a metal cap as the positive terminal: two different materials.
s: A cell needs two electrodes of different materials in an electrolyte
Both terminals here are zinc, so no electricity is produced
A real dry cell pairs zinc (negative) with a carbon rod and cap (positive)
